paragraphs.heading: Shallow water behind a barrier
paragraphs.text: A lagoon is a shallow body of water that a narrow landform cuts off from a larger one. The landform can be a reef, one or more barrier islands, a barrier peninsula or an isthmus. Lagoons are commonly divided into two kinds: coastal lagoons, also called barrier lagoons, and atoll lagoons. Around many parts of the world they are a common feature of the coast.

paragraphs.heading: Lagoon or estuary
paragraphs.text: Some bodies of water are classified both as coastal lagoons and as estuaries, and authorities do not agree on where the line falls. Some include fresh water bodies in the definition of a lagoon, while others restrict the word to water with some degree of salinity. Davis keeps the word for water that receives little or no fresh water and has little or no tidal flow, and he calls any bay with a regular inflow of fresh water an estuary. Kusky describes lagoons as normally elongated parallel to the coast. Estuaries, in his account, are usually drowned river valleys and are elongated perpendicular to the coast.

paragraphs.heading: How coastal lagoons form
paragraphs.text: Coastal lagoons form on coasts that slope gently, where barrier islands or reefs can develop offshore. The sea level must also be rising relative to the land along the shore. That can happen because the sea level itself rises, or because the land along the coast subsides. Coastal lagoons do not form on steep or rocky coasts, or where the tidal range is greater than 4 metres. Because the coast slopes gently, coastal lagoons are shallow.

paragraphs.heading: How atoll lagoons form
paragraphs.text: An atoll lagoon forms when tropical coral reefs grow upwards while the islands they surround subside. In the end only the reefs are left above sea level. Atoll lagoons often contain some deep portions, more than 20 m deep. In this they are unlike the lagoons that form on the shoreward side of fringing reefs.

paragraphs.heading: Young, changeable and common
paragraphs.text: Coastal lagoons are young and dynamic, and in geological terms they may be short-lived. If the sea level drops relative to the land, a lagoon may be left largely dry. If the sea level rises, the sea may breach or destroy barrier islands, and reefs may end up too deep underwater to protect the lagoon. Coastal lagoons are common: they occur along nearly 15 percent of the world's shorelines. In the United States, lagoons line over 75 percent of the Eastern and Gulf Coasts.

paragraphs.heading: Where the word comes from
paragraphs.text: The word lagoon comes from the Venetian łaguna, a word for the waters around Venice. That word in turn descends from Latin lacuna, a derivative of lacus, “lake”. William Dampier wrote in 1697 of a "Lagune or Lake of Salt water" on the Mexican coast. Many lagoons do not have “lagoon” in their common names. Several lagoons in the French Mediterranean are called étang, and several in Jutland are known as fjord.
